endorsements.quote: Strategies include fair learning algorithms minimizing reliance on demographic information by incorporating it into an alternative feature space, conducting external validations of algorithms—particularly using community-based (nonhospital) datasets—and performing prospective validations to identify potentially undiagnosed cases.
The latter involves proactive patient outreach to confirm diagnoses.

Responsible AI development must embed ethical guardrails, represent diverse populations, and account for real-world considerations, particularly in low-resource settings, with a special focus on implementation science.
Parker called for a more nuanced approach to AI implementation that addresses all these human factors so that AI technologies can truly support clinicians and enhance patient care in the age of AI.

unlisted_practices: Incorporate social and environmental context into AI model training and validation.
Use explainable AI frameworks in decision-support tools for complex and rare diseases to avoid masking uncertainty with simplistic binary outputs.
Maintain human oversight and expert curation of AI-flagged cases and LLM-generated content, ideally by subject matter experts.
Apply implementation science frameworks to identify barriers and facilitators to adopting AI in routine care.
Develop robust validation frameworks that address statistical challenges in rare disease research.
Ensure AI tools are adaptable and accessible across diverse health system architectures and low-resource settings.
Improve data accessibility, quality, and harmonization as a foundation for effective health care AI.
